title: Looking for collaborator to build a game on some pretty unique AI native tech
author: weichx
selftext:
I'm building a pretty unique piece of tech for AI coding and I'm looking for someone to collaborate with to build a little game on it.

[Wax](https://waxlang.dev) is a language that deterministically records how your game runs so any moment can be reproduced exactly on any machine, and that recording gets turned into something like a database that AI can query any moment of. 

  
The really exciting part is that these recordings become something like a database that AI can query and inspect.

This gives AI some pretty incredible capabilities for game development

* **Rewind and inspect gameplay**: AI can go back to any moment, inspect the actual game state, and understand exactly what happened.
* T**est and validate mechanics autonomously**: agents can play through a game, inspect the results, identify problems, and iterate.
* **Share entire playthroughs:** between AI agents, developers, or friends, with the exact same results on any machine, and any moment becomes forkable. 
* **Actually reproducible bug reports:** instead of trying to guess what went wrong from a screenshot or description, AI can replay the bug and inspect everything leading up to it.

This is not a video, its a live recording of real game state and any moment in your recording is perfectly reproducible across any platform and has an extremely small performance impact. For example if you make a game for Android and it has a bug, you can take that replay and run it on a PC byte-for-byte identically to how it ran on Android. 

  
See [https://waxlang.dev/doom](https://waxlang.dev/doom) for a demo of what this can do (safari isn't supported atm because they don't ship wasm multi memory yet, chrome & firefox are fine)

I'm now building a game engine on top of Wax with all the bells and whistles you'd expect of a modern engine. This is early days but I'm pretty excited about the potential and am interested in putting to the real test so I'm looking for someone to build with who could handle game design, art direction, game play mechanics and iterating on it to make it fun. I'd handle the engine level work. 

  
About me: I've built a couple game engines before, worked as a principal dev in big studios on the engine teams, have about 15 years of experience building deep tech: rendering systems, UI engines, compilers, AI behaviors / navigation, stuff like that. I have zero art / game design skills but all the skills to actually use that art and design and make it something awesomely playable.   


Let's make something great! 

Drop a comment or send me a DM if you want to talk more or see a more in depth demo of what this can do.

comments.author: speaks-with-stone
comments.body:
Sounds interesting!   
  
It's best practice to add user intent recording and use deterministic systems. Hard to playtest or have useful gameplay testing bots without it. It's just the right way to work.   
  
Why do you need a language for it, though? I read the FAQ and still not sure. I didn't read the whole site, apologies if there's an answer there already.

replies.author: weichx
replies.body:
This is its own language because there are a lot of tricky parts to determinism. floating point, garbage collection, hashing, cross platform quirks, etc. I also have a fully deterministic job/ecs system where thread count is not observable and runs identically everywhere. I also wanted full control end to end here, I own the language semantics, front end, machine code generation, and the full runtime / gc. All of these work together with a lot of tooling to make this all possible. It is not possible if we don't control any one of those pieces. I also designed this to sit inside another host language / game engine and work everywhere. Taking an existing language and trying to find a subset of it that was deterministic and ticked all the UX boxes was just not possible. 

I'm also able to ship the entire compiler toolchain in a recording which is \~5mb, so that it can be played anywhere and the compiler travels with the recording, which enables a lot of otherwise unachievable things. 

Not sure if you looked at the Doom demo (waxlang.dev/doom) but that is worth a peek to get a better idea of how this works.

replies.author: speaks-with-stone
replies.body:
The first time I looked at it, the demo just seemed like an image. Apparently I have to wait for some time before it becomes interactive.

I've played it now. Some of the loading (compiling and analyzing) was very slow while not showing progression, I thought it was stuck a few times. Still didn't understand the thing with changing the timeline - changing a value and rerunning made sense, but something about connecting things didn't.

So if I understand it correctly, what you wrote solves the pain of handling determinism yourself, wrapping the math functions, providing the timeline editor and such. So rather than handle determinism and recording the usual way, I would use Wax, and all my logic has to go through your runtime. Yes?

replies.author: weichx
replies.body:
yes, determinism is a promise of the language, and on top of that, any code written in wax is recorded. then that recording is inspectable, rewindable, editable (the grid replay w/ different game rules, same recording, new code playing against it). So you can effectively reconstruct the memory state at ANY point in time, AND do whatever you want with that. Add new code, gather some values, have an AI figure out for example "here's my replay, go find all the times I took damage, and tell me how close I was to each enemy, look for anomalies" or whatever you're interseted in. In the same vein, AI working on the game can run its own inspections and instead of guessing what happened or writing tests for isolated cases, can SEE into what you gave it, with real, live, inspectable data.

Did you see the part where in the replay you can click on the game and jump in and play from that moment live?

replies.author: speaks-with-stone
replies.body:
Yes. I fully understand the meaning of deterministic gameplay recording, this is the way I always work.   
  
I am still not entirely sure why a language, though. It's weird to me, doesn't sit right, like writing a language for implementing ECS or something. Why would I go to the trouble of taking on the issues of another language, just for something that's fairly simple to just do?

replies.author: speaks-with-stone
replies.body:
Let's say I use your language for my next game, rather than TS like I usually do.   
  
The cost is learning a new language, understanding how you go about things, and the inevitable problems that come from using code you didn't write.   
  
What would I gain from using Wax? Comfortable tooling once I get used to it?

Please feel free to ignore my curiosity :)

replies.author: weichx
replies.body:
I think we're talking about two different things.

Deterministic input replay is doable in TS, and if that's all you need, adopting another language isn't worth the cost. Wax goes further: a recording isn't just replayable inputs, it's a reconstructable, queryable, and forkable history of the program itself.

Say a player hits a weird bug an hour into a session and sends you the recording. With Wax, you can:

* Pull up the exact game state on any frame, on any machine.
* Write new inspection code *after* the fact, like finding every frame where an enemy saw the player and didn't attack, or some enemy got stuck on the nav mesh, without having logged it ahead of time.
* Query the whole recording like a database.
* Jump to the bug, swap in new logic, and branch execution from there.
* Hand the recording to an AI agent to write queries, test hypotheses, and verify fixes against real gameplay.

Pulling that off across machines requires language level guarantees around floats, memory, hashing, concurrency, host calls, and compiler optimizations. You don't have to rewrite your TS game, either, Wax can be embedded as the host handles the rest while Wax runs the stateful systems you want to record and dig into.

replies.author: speaks-with-stone
replies.body:
I get much of this functionality from having deterministic logic and input recordings. Trying hard to understand what the benefit is, it could be nice if there's a better way than my usual approach.

"Pull up the exact game state on any frame, on any machine." - what do you mean by on any machine? This seems to be the crux of the matter, no?

replies.author: weichx
replies.body:
I mean you can load a replay from an xbox to a pc, from an iphone to playstation, or from anywhere to web. And it always plays identically down to the byte.   
  
I don't know your setup, maybe you can get some of this with good discipline and strong engineering. The concepts aren't new, I've done the same thing at studios I've worked at too and it was always brittle, mostly worked, or worked in some cases but not others. 

  
The benefit is omniscience. It's literally impossible for a bug or scenario to not be reproducible.  The difference is that Wax makes these guarantees fundamental to the language and runtime, then builds tooling on top that lets you compile entirely new inspection code against an old recording, query arbitrary historical state, and fork execution with different logic.   
  
You don't need to log anything anymore. You don't need to ask for bug reports anymore, and your AI can do bug fixes/validation/iteration with perfect information instead of guessing from screenshots and log statements. 

Its not for everyone, it is a new language, its a new primitive in the dev toolbox really. I'm looking for people to battle test it with, if thats not you, no worries, I appreciate the discussion anyway.

replies.author: weichx
replies.body: [https://waxlang.dev/agent-demo](https://waxlang.dev/agent-demo) quick sample of an AI examining a recording and pulling out data from it.

replies.author: speaks-with-stone
replies.body:
OK, I think I finally understand.

You're digging the pit of success. If you're not used to strict determinism and it's not part of your work habit, this would be super useful. Like Unreal's blueprints or Unity's ECS, tools that are supposed to make the right way the easy way.

It's a good way of going about it. Not useful for me, as I already do this always by default. But I can absolutely see this doing a lot of good for younglings. 

Very cool, good luck and ganbatte ✨
